items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the distance of open water over which the wind blows to form waves”.
items.answer: Fetch
items.markingKey: Fetch: the distance of open water over which the wind blows to form waves. [1]

items.stem: Describe the differences between constructive and destructive waves.
items.answer: Constructive: low, long wavelength, 6-8 per minute, strong swash, weak backwash, build beaches. Destructive: high, steep, 13-15 per minute, weak swash, strong backwash, erode beaches.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each valid difference up to [3]

items.stem: Explain the process of longshore drift.
items.answer: Waves approach at an angle due to the prevailing wind; swash carries sediment up the beach at that angle; backwash returns it straight down under gravity; repeated, this moves sediment in a zig-zag along the coast.
items.markingKey: 1 mark angle of swash; 1 mark backwash at right angles; 1 mark zig-zag movement [3]

items.stem: Students measured longshore drift at a spit on the Gulf of Guinea coast. They placed a painted pebble at the water line and measured how far it had moved north after 20 minutes. Results for 4 trials (m): 7.7, 13.9, 7.8, 2. Calculate the mean rate of movement in metres per hour.

Students measured longshore drift at a beach near Lagos. They placed a painted pebble at the water line and measured how far it had moved west after 10 minutes. Results for 5 trials (m): 12.7, 5.9, 11.9, 11.1, 11.7. (a) Calculate the mean rate of movement in metres per hour. (b) Describe one safety precaution the students should take.
items.answer: (a) 64 m/h (b) Check tide times and work in groups away from cliffs; do not enter the water in rough conditions.

items.stem: Students measured longshore drift at a beach on the Black Sea coast. They placed a painted pebble at the water line and measured how far it had moved south after 15 minutes. Results for 5 trials (m): 7.5, 11.2, 7.8, 10.1, 12.2. (a) Calculate the mean distance moved. (b) Suggest two reasons why the results varied between trials.
items.answer: (a) 9.76 m (b) Changes in wave size or angle; the pebble may have been buried or moved by people; measurement error; different pebble sizes.

items.stem: Evaluate the view that wave type is the most important factor affecting the rate of coastal erosion. You may wish to consider: storms; beaches; rock type.
items.answer: For: Destructive waves with long fetch and storms cause rapid erosion. Against: Rock type and structure matter: soft boulder clay at Holderness erodes about 2 m a year while granite erodes very slowly. Beaches absorb wave energy; human defences and sub-aerial processes also affect rates. Judgement: Wave energy drives erosion, but geology often determines how fast it happens.
items.markingKey: Levels marking. Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple, generalised statements. Level 2 (4-6 marks): developed statements with some explanation and some reference to examples. Level 3 (7 marks): comprehensive, well-developed answer with accurate, place-specific detail and a clear judgement. [7]

items.answer: For: Destructive waves with long fetch and storms cause rapid erosion. Beaches absorb wave energy; human defences and sub-aerial processes also affect rates. Judgement: Wave energy drives erosion, but geology often determines how fast it happens.

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the movement of water up a beach after a wave breaks”.
items.answer: Swash
items.markingKey: Swash: the movement of water up a beach after a wave breaks. [1]

items.stem: Students measured longshore drift at a beach on the Black Sea coast. They placed a painted pebble at the water line and measured how far it had moved south after 15 minutes. Results for 5 trials (m): 10, 11, 10.7, 10.8, 3. (a) Suggest the direction of the prevailing wind. Explain your answer. (b) Suggest two reasons why the results varied between trials. (c) Describe one safety precaution the students should take.
items.answer: (a) From the north side (waves approach at an angle from the north): swash pushes sediment in the direction the waves travel, which is set by the prevailing wind. (b) Changes in wave size or angle; the pebble may have been buried or moved by people; measurement error; different pebble sizes. (c) Check tide times and work in groups away from cliffs; do not enter the water in rough conditions.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark direction; 1 mark explanation [2] (b) 1 mark each [2] (c) [1]

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “a section of hard rock that sticks out into the sea, with water on three sides”.
items.answer: Headland
items.markingKey: Headland: a section of hard rock that sticks out into the sea, with water on three sides. [1]

items.stem: Explain how a wave-cut platform forms.
items.answer: Waves erode the base of the cliff between high and low tide by hydraulic action and abrasion, forming a wave-cut notch; the overhang above collapses; the process repeats so the cliff retreats, leaving a gently sloping platform.
items.markingKey: 1 mark notch; 1 mark collapse; 1 mark retreat leaves platform [3]

items.stem: Explain how a stack forms from a headland.
items.answer: Waves erode a weakness (joint or fault) into a cave; caves on both sides meet to form an arch; the arch is widened and its roof is weakened by erosion and weathering until it collapses, leaving an isolated stack.
items.markingKey: 1 mark cave; 1 mark arch; 1 mark roof collapse [3]

items.stem: Fig. 4.1 describes the coast of Dorset, England. Bands of chalk and limestone (hard) alternate with clay and sand (soft), running at right angles to the coast. At Old Harry Rocks a chalk headland ends in two stacks and a stump; at Durdle Door there is a limestone arch; Swanage Bay is cut into soft clay. Suggest one way the landforms attract visitors and one problem visitors cause.
items.answer: Attraction: spectacular scenery, walking, photography, beaches. Problem: footpath erosion, litter, traffic congestion in summer.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Study Fig. 4.1, information about a discordant coastline in southern England. Hard chalk forms the headland at Handfast Point with the stacks of Old Harry Rocks; softer sands and clays form Studland Bay and Swanage Bay; further west a limestone arch stands at Durdle Door. (a) Suggest why the bays are wide and curved. (b) Suggest one way the landforms attract visitors and one problem visitors cause.
items.answer: (a) Soft clay and sand were eroded quickly; waves refract into the bay and spread energy, depositing sand to form a beach. (b) Attraction: spectacular scenery, walking, photography, beaches. Problem: footpath erosion, litter, traffic congestion in summer.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark rapid erosion; 1 mark deposition/wave refraction [2] (b) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Fig. 4.1 describes the coast of Dorset, England. Bands of chalk and limestone (hard) alternate with clay and sand (soft), running at right angles to the coast. At Old Harry Rocks a chalk headland ends in two stacks and a stump; at Durdle Door there is a limestone arch; Swanage Bay is cut into soft clay. (a) Name the landforms formed in soft and in hard rock. (b) Suggest why the bays are wide and curved.
items.answer: (a) Soft rock: bays (Swanage, Studland). Hard rock: headlands, arches, stacks and stumps. (b) Soft clay and sand were eroded quickly; waves refract into the bay and spread energy, depositing sand to form a beach.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark rapid erosion; 1 mark deposition/wave refraction [2]

items.stem: A student writes: “Stacks form before arches.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. An arch forms first; when its roof collapses a stack is left.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Study Fig. 4.1, information about a discordant coastline in southern England. Hard chalk forms the headland at Handfast Point with the stacks of Old Harry Rocks; softer sands and clays form Studland Bay and Swanage Bay; further west a limestone arch stands at Durdle Door. (a) Name the landforms formed in soft and in hard rock. (b) Explain the formation of Old Harry Rocks.
items.answer: (a) Soft rock: bays (Swanage, Studland). Hard rock: headlands, arches, stacks and stumps. (b) Hydraulic action and abrasion widened joints in the chalk headland into caves, then an arch; the arch collapsed, leaving stacks; a stack has been eroded to a stump.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark cave; 1 mark arch; 1 mark collapse [3]

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “an accumulation of sand and shingle deposited by waves between low tide and the highest storm waves”.
items.answer: Beach
items.markingKey: Beach: an accumulation of sand and shingle deposited by waves between low tide and the highest storm waves. [1]

items.stem: Explain how a spit forms.
items.answer: Longshore drift carries sediment along the coast; where the coast changes direction (e.g. at a river mouth), sediment continues to be deposited in the same direction into the sea, building a ridge; waves from another direction curve the end; salt marsh forms behind.
items.markingKey: 1 mark longshore drift; 1 mark change in coastline direction; 1 mark deposition builds out; 1 mark recurved end/salt marsh [4]

items.stem: Explain why a bar can form across a bay.
items.answer: Longshore drift extends a spit across the bay; if no strong river current cuts through, it joins the far headland, trapping a lagoon.
items.markingKey: 1 mark spit extends; 1 mark no river current; 1 mark lagoon [3]

items.stem: Study Fig. 4.2, which describes a spit. Material eroded from boulder-clay cliffs to the north is carried south by longshore drift. The spit extends across the mouth of an estuary, its end curves inland, and mudflats and salt marsh lie behind it. Explain why the spit has not grown across the estuary to form a bar.
items.answer: The river’s flow and tides scour the channel and carry sediment away.

items.stem: Study Fig. 4.2, which describes a spit. Material eroded from boulder-clay cliffs to the north is carried south by longshore drift. The spit extends across the mouth of an estuary, its end curves inland, and mudflats and salt marsh lie behind it. (a) State the direction of longshore drift shown in Fig. 4.2. (b) Explain why the end of the spit is curved.
items.answer: (a) Southwards. (b) Waves from a second direction (and the estuary currents) bend the tip inland.

items.stem: Evaluate the view that depositional coastal landforms such as spits and beaches are more easily damaged than erosional landforms. You may wish to consider: storms; human interference.
items.answer: For: Spits and beaches are made of loose sand and shingle that storms can remove quickly; cutting off sediment supply (e.g. groynes updrift) starves them. Against: Erosional landforms such as arches and stacks also collapse (e.g. Azure Window, Malta, 2017); spits can rebuild if sediment supply continues; dunes stabilised by vegetation are resilient. Judgement: Depositional landforms change faster and depend on sediment supply, so they are generally more fragile, though no coastal landform is permanent.
items.markingKey: Levels marking. Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple, generalised statements. Level 2 (4-6 marks): developed statements with some explanation and some reference to examples. Level 3 (7 marks): comprehensive, well-developed answer with accurate, place-specific detail and a clear judgement. [7]

items.stem: Explain why sand beaches are found in bays.
items.answer: Waves refract in bays, spreading their energy, so they are lower-energy constructive waves that deposit sand.
items.markingKey: 1 mark low energy; 1 mark deposition [2]

items.stem: Fig. 4.2 is a map of Spurn Head, a spit at the mouth of the Humber estuary in England. Longshore drift moves sediment south along the Holderness coast. The spit is about 5 km long, curves west at its tip, and has salt marsh on its sheltered western side. The River Humber flows east into the sea past the end of the spit. (a) State the direction of longshore drift shown in Fig. 4.2. (b) Explain why the end of the spit is curved. (c) Suggest how salt marsh has developed behind the spit.
items.answer: (a) Southwards. (b) Waves from a second direction (and the estuary currents) bend the tip inland. (c) Sheltered, calm water lets fine silt and mud settle; salt-tolerant plants colonise and trap more sediment.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] (b) [2] (c) 1 mark sheltered deposition; 1 mark vegetation [2]

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “a tiny animal with a soft body that builds a hard skeleton of calcium carbonate; colonies of polyps form reefs”.
items.answer: Coral polyp
items.markingKey: Coral polyp: a tiny animal with a soft body that builds a hard skeleton of calcium carbonate; colonies of polyps form reefs. [1]

items.stem: Describe the conditions needed for coral reefs to grow.
items.answer: Warm water (about 18-30 °C), clear and shallow (less than about 60 m) so light reaches the algae, salt water (no river water) and low sediment, and a solid base to grow on.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each condition up to [3]

items.stem: Explain the value of coral reefs to people.
items.answer: Fishing and food; tourism (diving, snorkelling) income and jobs; coastal protection by absorbing wave energy; medicines from reef species; high biodiversity.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each developed point up to [3]

items.stem: For the Great Barrier Reef, Australia or another example of a coral reef or mangrove ecosystem, briefly describe the value of the ecosystem to people.
items.answer: the Great Barrier Reef, Australia: About 2300 km long off Queensland; home to about 1500 fish species; tourism worth about AU$6 billion a year and about 64 000 jobs; protects the coast from waves.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a named, located example; up to 3 marks for accurate, place-specific points. Economic (fishing, tourism, products), social and environmental (biodiversity, coastal protection) value, with figures. [4]

items.stem: For the Sundarbans mangroves, Bangladesh and India or another example of a coral reef or mangrove ecosystem, briefly describe how the ecosystem is being managed sustainably.
items.answer: the Sundarbans mangroves, Bangladesh and India: UNESCO World Heritage site and reserves; limits on wood cutting; mangrove replanting; community forest management.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a named, located example; up to 3 marks for accurate, place-specific points. Protected areas, zoning, restrictions, replanting/restoration, community schemes. [4]

items.answer: Model answer (the Great Barrier Reef, Australia): Great Barrier Reef Marine Park zoning limits fishing and shipping; Reef 2050 Plan to reduce farm run-off; culling crown-of-thorns starfish; reef restoration trials.

Reef C: 27.3 °C, 1% bleached. Reef D: 26.5 °C, 0% bleached. Reef E: 29.3 °C, 35% bleached. Reef F: 30.4 °C, 70% bleached. Which reef had the most bleaching?
items.answer: Reef F

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “a concrete wall built along the coast to reflect wave energy and stop erosion and flooding”.
items.answer: Sea wall
items.markingKey: Sea wall: a concrete wall built along the coast to reflect wave energy and stop erosion and flooding. [1]

items.stem: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of a sea wall.
items.answer: Advantage: very effective at protecting buildings and roads behind it. Disadvantage: expensive (thousands of $ per metre), can be undermined by scouring, reflects energy and lowers the beach in front, looks unnatural.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Explain how managed retreat can be a sustainable option.
items.answer: Low-value farmland is allowed to flood, creating salt marsh that absorbs wave energy and provides habitats at little cost, instead of maintaining expensive defences.
items.markingKey: 1 mark allowing flooding; 1 mark natural defence/cheap [2]

items.stem: For the Holderness coast, England or another example of coastal management, briefly evaluate the strategies used to manage the coast.
items.answer: the Holderness coast, England: Mappleton’s defences protected the village and the coast road, but trapped sediment so cliffs to the south eroded faster; protecting the whole coast would cost far more than the value of the farmland, so the shoreline management plan defends only towns.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a named, located example; up to 3 marks for accurate, place-specific points. Successes and problems (cost, effects downdrift, environment), with a judgement. [4]

items.stem: For the Holderness coast, England or another example of coastal management, briefly describe the strategies used to manage the coast.
items.answer: the Holderness coast, England: The boulder-clay coast erodes about 2 m a year; at Mappleton (1991) about £2 million was spent on two rock groynes and rock armour; Hornsea and Withernsea have sea walls and groynes; other stretches are left undefended.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a named, located example; up to 3 marks for accurate, place-specific points. Named hard and soft strategies, with locations, costs and dates. [4]

items.stem: Name an example of coastal management. For your chosen example, describe the strategies used to manage the coast.
items.answer: Model answer (the Holderness coast, England): The boulder-clay coast erodes about 2 m a year; at Mappleton (1991) about £2 million was spent on two rock groynes and rock armour; Hornsea and Withernsea have sea walls and groynes; other stretches are left undefended.

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the movement of water back down a beach towards the sea under gravity”.
items.answer: Backwash
items.markingKey: Backwash: the movement of water back down a beach towards the sea under gravity. [1]

items.stem: Explain how hydraulic action erodes a cliff.
items.answer: Breaking waves force water and air into cracks; the air is compressed and, when the wave retreats, expands explosively, widening the cracks until pieces break off.
items.markingKey: 1 mark compressed air in cracks; 1 mark repeated widening [2]

items.stem: Students measured longshore drift at a spit on the Gulf of Guinea coast. They placed a painted pebble at the water line and measured how far it had moved north after 15 minutes. Results for 4 trials (m): 7.8, 2.9, 11.2, 5.5. Calculate the mean rate of movement in metres per hour.

Students measured longshore drift at a spit on the Gulf of Guinea coast. They placed a painted pebble at the water line and measured how far it had moved north after 20 minutes. Results for 5 trials (m): 4.6, 13.4, 4.9, 8.8, 9.5. (a) Calculate the mean rate of movement in metres per hour. (b) Describe one safety precaution the students should take.
items.answer: (a) 24.7 m/h (b) Check tide times and work in groups away from cliffs; do not enter the water in rough conditions.

items.answer: For: Destructive waves with long fetch and storms cause rapid erosion. Against: Rock type and structure matter: soft boulder clay at Holderness erodes about 2 m a year while granite erodes very slowly. Beaches absorb wave energy; human defences and sub-aerial processes also affect rates. Judgement: Wave energy drives erosion, but geology often determines how fast it happens.

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “a wide, curved inlet of the sea between two headlands, formed where softer rock is eroded”.
items.answer: Bay
items.markingKey: Bay: a wide, curved inlet of the sea between two headlands, formed where softer rock is eroded. [1]

items.stem: Explain why headlands and bays form on a discordant coastline.
items.answer: Soft rock (e.g. clay) is eroded quickly to form bays; hard rock (e.g. chalk, limestone) is more resistant and is left sticking out as headlands.
items.markingKey: 1 mark differential erosion; 1 mark hard/soft outcome [2]

items.stem: At Happisburgh, England, the cliff edge retreated 11 m between 1990 and 2000. Explain why soft cliffs such as boulder clay retreat quickly.
items.answer: Clay is weak and easily eroded by waves; rain saturates it, causing slumping; eroded material is easily washed away so the cliff base is not protected.
items.markingKey: 1 mark weak rock; 1 mark slumping/weathering [2]

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that rock type is the most important factor in the formation of erosional coastal landforms? Use examples you have studied. You may wish to consider: joints and faults; hard and soft rock.
items.answer: For: Headlands and bays form where hard and soft rocks alternate (Dorset); joints and faults in chalk and limestone are eroded into caves, arches and stacks. Against: Wave energy, fetch and storms supply the erosive power; sub-aerial weathering weakens cliffs and arch roofs; sea-level change and human defences also matter. Judgement: Rock type and structure control where and what landforms develop, but wave energy determines how fast they form.
items.markingKey: Levels marking. Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple, generalised statements. Level 2 (4-6 marks): developed statements with some explanation and some reference to examples. Level 3 (7 marks): comprehensive, well-developed answer with accurate, place-specific detail and a clear judgement. [7]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “beach”?
options: A ridge of sand or shingle that extends across a bay, joining two headlands and trapping a lagoon behind it.
A ridge of sand or shingle that joins an island to the mainland.
A long, narrow ridge of sand or shingle joined to the land at one end and extending out to sea, formed by longshore drift.
An accumulation of sand and shingle deposited by waves between low tide and the highest storm waves.
items.answer: An accumulation of sand and shingle deposited by waves between low tide and the highest storm waves.
items.markingKey: Beach: an accumulation of sand and shingle deposited by waves between low tide and the highest storm waves. [1]

items.stem: Explain why a river mouth can prevent a spit from becoming a bar.
items.answer: The river’s flow carries sediment away and keeps the channel open, so the spit cannot join the opposite shore.
items.markingKey: 1 mark river current; 1 mark keeps gap open [2]

items.stem: Students measured the profile of a beach beside a spit from the sea to the back of the beach in 5 sections each 5 m long. Slope angles (°): 3, 6, 2, 6, 4. Mean pebble size (mm) for each section: 13, 42, 48, 69, 76. Describe how the students should have measured the slope angle.
items.answer: Two ranging poles placed at each break of slope (or every 5/10 m); a clinometer used to sight between equal heights on the poles; distance measured with a tape.
items.markingKey: 1 mark ranging poles/tape; 1 mark clinometer [2]

items.stem: Students measured the profile of a shingle beach from the sea to the back of the beach in 5 sections each 10 m long. Slope angles (°): 2, 5, 8, 10, 5. Mean pebble size (mm) for each section: 31, 43, 46, 73, 83. (a) Calculate the mean slope angle. (b) Explain why larger pebbles are found at the back of the beach. (c) Describe how the students should have measured the slope angle.
items.answer: (a) 6° (b) Only powerful storm-wave swash can throw large pebbles high up the beach; the weak backwash cannot carry them back down. (c) Two ranging poles placed at each break of slope (or every 5/10 m); a clinometer used to sight between equal heights on the poles; distance measured with a tape.
items.markingKey: (a) 30 ÷ 5 = 6° [1] (b) 1 mark storm swash; 1 mark weak backwash [2] (c) 1 mark ranging poles/tape; 1 mark clinometer [2]

items.stem: A student writes: “Coral reefs can grow in deep, cold water as long as there are waves.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Reef-building corals need warm, shallow, clear water so that their algae can photosynthesise.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain how mangroves protect coastlines.
items.answer: Dense roots slow waves and storm surges, trap sediment and reduce erosion, so cyclones such as Sidr (2007) caused less damage behind mangroves.
items.markingKey: 1 mark absorb energy; 1 mark trap sediment [2]

items.stem: Study your case study of a coral reef or mangrove ecosystem (for example the Sundarbans mangroves, Bangladesh and India). Briefly describe how the ecosystem is being managed sustainably.
items.answer: the Sundarbans mangroves, Bangladesh and India: UNESCO World Heritage site and reserves; limits on wood cutting; mangrove replanting; community forest management.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a named, located example; up to 3 marks for accurate, place-specific points. Protected areas, zoning, restrictions, replanting/restoration, community schemes. [4]

items.stem: Table 4.1 shows maximum sea surface temperature and the percentage of coral bleached at reef sites in one summer. Reef A: 26.9 °C, 0% bleached. Reef B: 31.4 °C, 80% bleached. Reef C: 31.1 °C, 85% bleached. Reef D: 29.8 °C, 54% bleached. Reef E: 27.5 °C, 0% bleached. (a) Describe the relationship between temperature and bleaching. (b) Explain why high temperatures cause bleaching. (c) Suggest two other human activities that damage coral reefs.
items.answer: (a) Positive correlation: higher sea temperatures are linked to more bleaching, especially above about 28-29 °C. (b) Heat stress makes the coral expel its zooxanthellae algae, which give it food and colour; without them it turns white and may starve. (c) Pollution and sediment from farms and building; overfishing and blast fishing; tourist damage by divers and anchors; coral mining.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark positive; 1 mark use of data [2] (b) 1 mark algae expelled; 1 mark loss of food/colour [2] (c) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: A student writes: “Hard engineering is always the best way to protect a coastline.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. It is expensive and can cause problems elsewhere; soft engineering or managed retreat may be cheaper and more sustainable.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: A council must protect 600 m of coast in front of a fishing village; the property protected is worth about $50 million. Table 4.2: Rock armour: $1 500 per metre, lasts about 30 years. Beach nourishment: $500 per metre, lasts about 5 years. Groynes: $2 000 per metre, lasts about 25 years. Is the scheme worth paying for? Use the figures to support your answer.
items.answer: Every option costs much less than the $50 million of property protected (most expensive $1.2 million), so protection is justified economically.
items.markingKey: 1 mark judgement; 1 mark data [2]

items.stem: A council must protect 2000 m of coast in front of a coastal village with a caravan park; the property protected is worth about $80 million. Table 4.2: Beach nourishment: $800 per metre, lasts about 5 years. Rock armour: $2 500 per metre, lasts about 30 years. Groynes: $1 500 per metre, lasts about 25 years. (a) Calculate the total cost of each option. (b) Calculate the cost per year of life for each option and identify the cheapest per year.
items.answer: (a) beach nourishment: $1.6 million; rock armour: $5 million; groynes: $3 million (b) beach nourishment: $0.32 million/yr; rock armour: $0.167 million/yr; groynes: $0.12 million/yr. Cheapest: groynes.
items.markingKey: (a) cost per metre × length for each [2] (b) 1 mark total ÷ life; 1 mark correct choice [2]

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “a low, gentle wave with a strong swash and weak backwash that builds up beaches”.
items.answer: Constructive wave
items.markingKey: Constructive wave: a low, gentle wave with a strong swash and weak backwash that builds up beaches. [1]

items.stem: Explain why erosion is greatest during storms.
items.answer: Strong winds create large, destructive waves with more energy; they hurl more sediment at the cliffs (abrasion) and hydraulic action is greater.
items.markingKey: 1 mark larger waves; 1 mark more abrasion/hydraulic action [2]

items.stem: Students measured longshore drift at a beach on the Black Sea coast. They placed a painted pebble at the water line and measured how far it had moved south after 10 minutes. Results for 4 trials (m): 13.5, 13.6, 10.5, 9.9. Suggest two reasons why the results varied between trials.
items.answer: Changes in wave size or angle; the pebble may have been buried or moved by people; measurement error; different pebble sizes.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Students measured longshore drift at Holderness, England. They placed a painted pebble at the water line and measured how far it had moved east after 15 minutes. Results for 5 trials (m): 8, 4, 8.5, 8.4, 5.3. (a) Suggest the direction of the prevailing wind. Explain your answer. (b) Describe one safety precaution the students should take.
items.answer: (a) From the west side (waves approach at an angle from the west): swash pushes sediment in the direction the waves travel, which is set by the prevailing wind. (b) Check tide times and work in groups away from cliffs; do not enter the water in rough conditions.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark direction; 1 mark explanation [2] (b) [1]

items.stem: Evaluate the view that wave type is the most important factor affecting the rate of coastal erosion. You may wish to consider: fetch; storms.
items.answer: For: Destructive waves with long fetch and storms cause rapid erosion. Against: Rock type and structure matter: soft boulder clay at Holderness erodes about 2 m a year while granite erodes very slowly. Beaches absorb wave energy; human defences and sub-aerial processes also affect rates. Judgement: Wave energy drives erosion, but geology often determines how fast it happens.
items.markingKey: Levels marking. Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple, generalised statements. Level 2 (4-6 marks): developed statements with some explanation and some reference to examples. Level 3 (7 marks): comprehensive, well-developed answer with accurate, place-specific detail and a clear judgement. [7]

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “an undercut at the base of a cliff between high and low tide, eroded by waves”.
items.answer: Wave-cut notch
items.markingKey: Wave-cut notch: an undercut at the base of a cliff between high and low tide, eroded by waves. [1]

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “Headlands are made of more resistant rock than bays.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. Hard rock erodes more slowly than the soft rock in bays.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: At a sandstone cliff on the Black Sea coast, the cliff edge retreated 13 m between 2000 and 2020. Explain why soft cliffs such as boulder clay retreat quickly.
items.answer: Clay is weak and easily eroded by waves; rain saturates it, causing slumping; eroded material is easily washed away so the cliff base is not protected.
items.markingKey: 1 mark weak rock; 1 mark slumping/weathering [2]

items.stem: Fig. 4.1 describes the coast of Dorset, England. Bands of chalk and limestone (hard) alternate with clay and sand (soft), running at right angles to the coast. At Old Harry Rocks a chalk headland ends in two stacks and a stump; at Durdle Door there is a limestone arch; Swanage Bay is cut into soft clay. (a) Explain the formation of Old Harry Rocks. (b) Suggest why the bays are wide and curved. (c) Suggest one way the landforms attract visitors and one problem visitors cause.
items.answer: (a) Hydraulic action and abrasion widened joints in the chalk headland into caves, then an arch; the arch collapsed, leaving stacks; a stack has been eroded to a stump. (b) Soft clay and sand were eroded quickly; waves refract into the bay and spread energy, depositing sand to form a beach. (c) Attraction: spectacular scenery, walking, photography, beaches. Problem: footpath erosion, litter, traffic congestion in summer.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark cave; 1 mark arch; 1 mark collapse [3] (b) 1 mark rapid erosion; 1 mark deposition/wave refraction [2] (c) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “spit”?
options: The curved tip of a spit formed when waves from a different direction bend the end inland.
A ridge of sand or shingle that extends across a bay, joining two headlands and trapping a lagoon behind it.
A ridge of sand or shingle that joins an island to the mainland.
A long, narrow ridge of sand or shingle joined to the land at one end and extending out to sea, formed by longshore drift.
items.answer: A long, narrow ridge of sand or shingle joined to the land at one end and extending out to sea, formed by longshore drift.
items.markingKey: Spit: a long, narrow ridge of sand or shingle joined to the land at one end and extending out to sea, formed by longshore drift. [1]

items.stem: A student writes: “Spits form where destructive waves are eroding the coast.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Spits are depositional; they need a supply of sediment and longshore drift.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Students measured the profile of a beach near Muscat from the sea to the back of the beach in 6 sections each 5 m long. Slope angles (°): 5, 2, 12, 15, 15, 2. Mean pebble size (mm) for each section: 15, 25, 59, 73, 77, 79. (a) Calculate the mean slope angle. (b) Identify the steepest section.

Study Fig. 4.2, which describes a spit. Material eroded from boulder-clay cliffs to the north is carried south by longshore drift. The spit extends across the mouth of an estuary, its end curves inland, and mudflats and salt marsh lie behind it. (a) State the direction of longshore drift shown in Fig. 4.2. (b) Explain why the end of the spit is curved. (c) Explain why the spit has not grown across the estuary to form a bar.
items.answer: (a) Southwards. (b) Waves from a second direction (and the estuary currents) bend the tip inland. (c) The river’s flow and tides scour the channel and carry sediment away.

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “Mangroves are adapted to grow in salty water.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. They have salt-filtering roots or excrete salt through their leaves.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain why mangrove swamps are being destroyed.
items.answer: Cleared for shrimp farms, rice, tourism resorts, ports and housing; cut for firewood and charcoal; polluted by oil and waste.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each reason up to [3]

items.stem: Name one example of a coral reef or mangrove ecosystem you have studied and, for that example, describe the value of the ecosystem to people.
items.answer: the Sundarbans mangroves, Bangladesh and India: About 10 000 km² of mangroves in the Ganges-Brahmaputra delta; habitat for Bengal tigers and fish nurseries; timber, honey and fishing for millions; protection from cyclones and storm surges.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a named, located example; up to 3 marks for accurate, place-specific points. Economic (fishing, tourism, products), social and environmental (biodiversity, coastal protection) value, with figures. [4]

items.stem: Table 4.1 shows maximum sea surface temperature and the percentage of coral bleached at reef sites in one summer. Reef A: 28.9 °C, 33% bleached. Reef B: 29.8 °C, 48% bleached. Reef C: 29.3 °C, 33% bleached. Reef D: 30.1 °C, 50% bleached. Reef E: 28.8 °C, 27% bleached. Reef F: 31.2 °C, 76% bleached. (a) Describe the relationship between temperature and bleaching. (b) Explain why high temperatures cause bleaching. (c) Suggest two other human activities that damage coral reefs.
items.answer: (a) Positive correlation: higher sea temperatures are linked to more bleaching, especially above about 28-29 °C. (b) Heat stress makes the coral expel its zooxanthellae algae, which give it food and colour; without them it turns white and may starve. (c) Pollution and sediment from farms and building; overfishing and blast fishing; tourist damage by divers and anchors; coral mining.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark positive; 1 mark use of data [2] (b) 1 mark algae expelled; 1 mark loss of food/colour [2] (c) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “Rock armour absorbs wave energy.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. Gaps between the boulders absorb and break up waves, reducing erosion.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: A council must protect 400 m of coast in front of a seaside town; the property protected is worth about $30 million. Table 4.2: Groynes: $2 000 per metre, lasts about 25 years. Sea wall: $8 000 per metre, lasts about 50 years. Rock armour: $1 500 per metre, lasts about 30 years. Is the scheme worth paying for? Use the figures to support your answer.
items.answer: Every option costs much less than the $30 million of property protected (most expensive $3.2 million), so protection is justified economically.
items.markingKey: 1 mark judgement; 1 mark data [2]

items.stem: For coastal protection in the Maldives or another example of coastal management, briefly describe the strategies used to manage the coast.
items.answer: coastal protection in the Maldives: Most islands are less than 1.5 m above sea level; Malé is surrounded by a 3 m concrete sea wall and tetrapods built with Japanese aid; Hulhumalé, a new artificial island about 2 m above sea level, is being built for housing; coral reef protection.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a named, located example; up to 3 marks for accurate, place-specific points. Named hard and soft strategies, with locations, costs and dates. [4]
